prompt: Walk through how Insertion Sort would sort [3, 1, 2].
answer_markdown: Start with [3] as the sorted part. Take 1: it's smaller than 3, so shift 3 right and place 1 first → [1, 3]. Take 2: it's smaller than 3 but bigger than 1, so shift 3 right and place 2 between them → [1, 2, 3]. Each new element only moves as far left as it needs to, which is why Insertion Sort is fast when the array is already close to sorted.

prompt: Why is Selection Sort's time complexity O(n²) even though it only makes O(n) swaps?
answer_markdown: Time complexity counts all the work, not just swaps. For each of the n positions, Selection Sort scans the entire remaining unsorted portion to find the minimum — that scan itself takes O(n) time, and you do it n times, giving O(n²) comparisons. The swap count staying low doesn't change the total work of finding what to swap.

prompt: Given a nearly-sorted array of a million elements with only a few items out of place, which of Bubble, Selection, or Insertion Sort would you pick, and why?
answer_markdown: Insertion Sort. It can finish close to O(n) on nearly-sorted input because each element only shifts a few positions before landing in place, so the inner while loop exits almost immediately most of the time. Selection Sort ignores existing order entirely and always does the full O(n²) scan, and Bubble Sort needs the early-exit optimization to get any benefit at all — and even then does more comparisons than Insertion Sort in practice.
